planting.note: Set out divisions or container plants in spring or early fall into humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Fire Dragon is a David's epimedium hybrid that spreads into a tidy semi-evergreen groundcover patch within two to three seasons.

directions: Fire Dragon is a hybrid of Epimedium davidii and E. leptorrhizum prized for its unusually large, bicolor flowers, which combine bright yellow inner petals with striking purplish-pink outer sepals on wiry stems held above the foliage in mid to late spring. New leaves emerge tinged with bronze and amber before settling into a semi-evergreen mid-green mound that holds up through winter in milder climates. It thrives in medium to full shade with humus-rich, well-drained soil and, once its rhizomes are established after a season or two, tolerates the dry shade found under mature trees and shrubs. Shear off tattered old foliage in late winter before the flower spikes emerge so the spring bloom show is not hidden by ragged leaves.

common_name: Pierre's Purple Epimedium (Large Wine-Purple Fairy Wings)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown crowns in spring or early fall in fertile, humus-rich soil in part to full shade; Pierre's Purple is a deciduous longspur epimedium selection whose new bronze-purple foliage appears just ahead of the flowers each spring.

directions: Pierre's Purple was selected from Epimedium grandiflorum for having the largest, most saturated wine-purple flowers of the longspur epimediums, each bloom trimmed with slender white-tipped spurs and held in loose sprays above the emerging foliage in mid-spring. The first flush of leaves opens bronze-purple before maturing to bright green for the rest of the season, giving two distinct seasonal looks from the same clump. It is a deciduous, deer-resistant perennial best suited to woodland gardens, shaded borders, and pathways beneath trees, where it slowly builds into a dense, weed-suppressing patch. Grow it in humus-rich, well-drained soil with consistent moisture while establishing, then divide crowded clumps after flowering every four to five years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Set out divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained soil in part to full shade; Cherry Tart is a slow-spreading versicolor hybrid best used where its emerging russet-purple foliage and pink flowers can be seen up close.

directions: Cherry Tart stands out among Epimedium x versicolor selections for flowers that lean deep into rose-pink rather than the typical yellow tones of the group, each bloom a starburst of pink spurs surrounding a paler, yellow-edged cup. The rounded leaflets emerge a rich russet-purple in spring and hold that color longer than most epimediums before shifting toward green, then take on bronze tints again as the semi-evergreen foliage persists through a mild winter. It spreads more slowly than many of its relatives, so it stays useful as a well-behaved edger along shaded paths or at the front of a woodland border rather than as an aggressive groundcover. Grow in humus-rich, well-drained to slightly dry soil in part to full shade, and comb out old foliage in late winter just before the new flower spikes appear.
